evidence.title: A National Cross-Sectional Survey of Artificial Intelligence Patient Safety Reporting Infrastructure Available to US Nurses
evidence.outcome: Presence of a designated mechanism for end users to report AI anomalies
evidence.effect: 83 of 424 nurses (19.6%) with an AI-related safety concern had no formal reporting channel; odds were 2.54 times higher in non-hospital settings.
evidence.quote: Among 424 nurses who encountered an AI-related patient safety concern, 83 (19.6%) reported no formal channel for reporting it.

commentary.bottom_line: Five guidance sources endorse a designated reporting mechanism for AI anomalies, but no study has tested whether such a mechanism increases reporting or leads to corrective action. One survey found that 83 of 424 nurses (19.6%) who had an AI-related safety concern had no formal channel to report it.

perspectives.view: No study compares settings with and without a designated reporting mechanism, so certainty cannot be rated for the practice itself. The single cross-sectional survey documents a gap in reporting channels. It does not measure whether a channel, assigned responders, or traceability change reporting rates, response times, or patient outcomes. The endorsements rest on expert consensus.

About one in five nurses with an AI safety concern reported having no formal channel, which suggests some frontline observations of AI error may never reach anyone able to act. Whether a designated mechanism would catch those errors before they reach patients remains untested, and the survey did not follow concerns to any harm.

The odds of lacking a reporting channel were 2.54 times higher in non-hospital settings. This may mean ambulatory and other outpatient sites need separate attention when a system sets up AI reporting. No study reports the staffing, cost, or response workload of running such a mechanism with assigned responders.

The survey sampled nurses in the United States and did not report whether respondents worked in safety-net, Medicaid-serving, or other under-resourced settings. The higher odds of missing channels outside hospitals may bear on community clinics, but the data do not show this directly.

One endorsing commentary calls for reporting pathways open to users and caregivers as well as clinicians. The only available study surveyed nurses, so no evidence describes whether patients can report AI errors, whether they receive a response, or how reporting affects their trust.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare reporting volume, time to response, error correction, and downstream harm before and after a designated AI reporting mechanism is introduced, including outpatient and non-hospital sites and pathways open to patients and caregivers.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tests the practice, and the one hazard survey did not report whether it included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no evidence on whether reporting mechanisms work in their settings or reach their patients.
